catalog_quote: Most conspicuous among the many developments which characterize Northern Paman reflection of Proto Paman is the reduction of Initial syllables (*CV1) by loss of initial consonants (*C1) and loss or other reduction of immediately following vowels (*V1). Associated with initial reduction, and at least partially responsible for it is a shift of primary stress (a strictly phonetic feature) from the initial to the second syllable (*CV2) in Paman stems. In all Northern Paman languages, except Uraði and its sister dialects, *C1 was lost invariably. ... Short *V1 was lost in some languages, retained in others, and metathesized in still others. Long *V·1 was shortened in all. [pp. 167-168] ... Word stress in [Linngithigh] is predictable: the first vowel which is preceded by a consonant is stressed. Accordingly, the first vowel is stressed in words beginning in a consonant or cluster ... but the second vowel in words which begin in a vowel [p. 179; sister language, not Mbiywom] ... Languages where stress has shifted from first to second syllable, leaving unstressed initial syllables, include Mpalitjanh, Yinwum, Linngithigh, Anguthimri, Ngkoth, Mbiywom, ... [Blevins 2001: 484, secondary] ... Northern Paman (all with stress shift) ... Mbiywom invariable Hale (1964, 1976a) [Blevins 2001: 487 appendix]
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (symlink to) via its text (lines 8223-8245) and viewed the page scan AL 8(2) p. 167) and p. 168). The quoted passage is on those pages exactly as reported, the only differences being typographic: the scan prints "reduction of Initial syllables" with a capital I, the subscripts in *CV1/*C1/*V1/*CV2 are set as subscripts, and "loss o[r] other reduction" has a smudged letter that the scanned reads as "of" (the compiler "or" is the grammatical reading). Page 167 ends at "..second syllable (*CV2) in" and p. 168 begins "Paman stems." then "In all Northern Paman languages, except Uraði and its sister dialects, *C1 was lost invariably." Locator pp. 167-168 = pp. 170-171 is correct. Identity:…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Historical, subgroup-level: in all Northern Paman languages (Mbiywom included) primary stress moved from the first to the second syllable of the Proto-Paman stem, and the unstressed initial consonant (and often its vowel) was then lost. Synchronically this puts stress on the etymological second syllable, i.e. the first vowel that follows a consonant (the rule Hale states explicitly only for Linngithigh, p.179: 'the first vowel which is preceded by a consonant is stressed'); a modern vowel-initial Mbiywom word would thus be stressed on its second vowel, a consonant-initial one on its first.
new_statements.exceptions: None for stress. For initial-consonant loss Uradhi and its sister dialects are the exception; Mbiywom is among the languages with invariable *C1 loss (also Blevins 2001 p.487 table).
new_statements.domain_note: Diachronic statement about Paman stems (word-level); Hale calls stress 'a strictly phonetic feature'. No Mbiywom forms are stress-marked in Hale 1966 or in Dixon 1980's Mbiywom examples (/two/ 'dog', /ngwu/ 'knee'). Group-level scope, so low confidence for Mbiywom itself; Blevins 2001 (secondary) explicitly names Mbiywom among 'languages where stress has shifted from first to second syllable'.
new_statements.identity_note: Hale's Mbiywom (self-name, cp. /mbiy/ 'camp') = McConnel 1939 Mbeiwum, Sharp 1939 Kok Mbewan, Tindale 1974 Mbewum; AIATSIS Y41; called Wik-Ompom in Wik-Mungkan (Sutton & Hale 2021; Austlang says Mbiywom and Wik Ompom Y48 may be the same language). The quoted statement is Hale's group-level historical statement for the whole Northern Paman subgroup (his 13-variety sample includes Mbiywom, AL 8(2) p.163, survey entry p.166); no source examined gives a Mbiywom-specific stress rule. The only language-specific synchronic rule in the same article is for the sister language Linngithigh (leni1238), p.179.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (byte-identical to the copy consulted; 18 pp., ProQuest scan, text = cover line only) and its scanned Rendered PDF page 9 (= p. 256) to an image and read it: the first paragraph of section 2 is exactly as quoted ('Most conspicuous among the many developments.. is a shift of primary stress (a strictly phonetic feature) from the initial to the second syllable (*CV2) in Paman stems.'); the only differences are typographic: the original has subscripts *CV₁, *C₁, *V₁, *CV₂ (reader wrote '*C V1' etc.) and spells the language 'Uraδi' (reader: 'Uradi'). The second sentence 'In all Northern Paman languages, except Uraδi and its sister dialects, *C₁ was lost invariably.' is on the same page sc…
new_statements.relation_note: The deciding sentence is the same sentence (near-verbatim) already recorded as the existing statement from Hale 1966 (AL 8(2), pp. 167-168), so it agrees with that statement and adds nothing new about placement; it is a Northern Paman group-level, diachronic statement (stress on the second syllable of the Proto-Paman stem; stress strictly phonetic/non-contrastive), not a Mbiywom-specific synchronic description. Relative to the catalog record (classification segmental, empty rule) it supplies the same Hale stress statement, i.e. it refines the empty rule rather than contradicting anything. No Mbiywom words with marked stress appear in the paper (only ŋkwu 'knee', kwu 'tree' on p. 260).
new_statements.rule_in_words: A group-level, diachronic statement for all 13 Northern Paman languages (Mbiywom included as subgroup H): primary stress, described as 'a strictly phonetic feature' (i.e. non-contrastive), shifted from the initial to the second syllable of the Proto-Paman stem, and this shift drove the loss of the initial consonant and the loss/metathesis of the initial vowel. Since Mbiywom belongs to the languages south of Mpalityan/Lutiy in which short *V1 was 'ordinarily lost' (except where metathesised to a glide, e.g. *puŋku > ŋkwu 'knee', *yuku > kwu 'tree', p. 260), the stressed proto-second syllable is normally the first syllable of the modern Mbiywom word; the paper does not state a synchronic Mbiywom stress rule in those terms.
new_statements.exceptions: Uradhi (and sister dialects) retained *C1 sometimes and never lost or metathesised short *V1; Mpalityan and Lutiy sometimes lost, retained or metathesised *V1; for Mbiywom specifically (with Aritinŋitiy) *u metathesised from *CV1 even where *V2 was also *u (p. 260). No exceptions to the stress statement itself are given.
new_statements.identity_note: Hale 1964, p. 254: 'Mbiywom (cp. /mbiy/ camp) was spoken on the middle and upper Watson River and, more recently, on Myall Creek. York Downs and Merluna cattle stations are regarded by informants as being in Mbiywom country. The term is easily identified in the published literature (Mbeiwum, McConnel, 1939; Kok Mbewan, Sharp, 1939).' It is subgroup (H) on its own among the 13 Northern Paman samples recorded by Hale in 1960 from informants at Weipa and Aurukun Missions; it shares the fewest cognates with the rest of Northern Paman (average 38/100, p. 262).
